newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechnya sets inauguration day of new leader.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya sets inauguration day of new leader.

text.p: Officials in rebel Chechnya were laying plans on Thursday for inaugurating Aslan Maskhadov as president, three days after the former guerrilla leader won a big majority in a presidential poll.
Interfax news agency quoted Maskhadov aide Ruslan Kutayev as saying the inauguration ceremony would take place on February 10, after the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan ends.

The latest incomplete returns showed that Maskhadov, the rebels' chief-of-staff during a 21-month conflict with Russian troops, won nearly two-thirds of the vote in Monday's election, described by international observers as fair.
Final official results are expected at the weekend.

But the separatists faced potential turmoil from within their own ranks after a hardline rebel who led a bloody hostage raid a year ago said he did not recognise the poll and was planning terror attacks on Russia.
"At least three Russian cities must be burned to cinders," Salman Raduyev told Reuters on Wednesday. "We are working on a major operation codenamed 'Ash'."

Raduyev led a group of fighters which seized hostages in the town of Kizlyar in Russia's Dagestan region, which borders Chechnya. He has repeatedly threatened to attack targets outside Chechnya since then.
Speaking in his village in eastern Chechnya, he said he would not obey the new Chechen president, who is widely regarded as a moderate. He vowed to carry out his own war against Russia.
Chechen leaders declared their region independent in 1991, provoking a bitter dispute with Russia which flared into heavy fighting three years later.
Troops sent into the region in December 1994 failed to seize full control and Russia pulled the last of the soldiers out this month.
Tens of thousands of people, most of them civilians, were killed in the fighting in Chechnya, a region with more than one million people before the conflict.

Maskhadov, a former Soviet army colonel, defeated acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev and 11 other candidates in the election, which the Chechens see as a way of cementing their de facto independence from Russia.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Maskhadov as saying he wanted discussions about Chechnya's status to begin "as soon as possible".

Maskhadov agreed in August with Russia's then national security adviser, Alexander Lebed, that decisions on the status of the mountainous region be postponed for five years. Moscow has refused to countenance the idea of an independent Chechnya.
But Maskhadov and other Chechens say the region is already independent and needs only recognition from the outside world to seal that fact.
A Russian foreign ministry official said at the weekend that Moscow would sever diplomatic ties with any country which recognises Chechnya.
